OpenAI built Control Room, a central system to track model workloads across its research infrastructure and stop them quickly on safety or security concerns (4,085 likes).

OpenAI@OpenAI
We built Control Room, a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.

It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job.

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach for safe frontier model training and deployment.

Artificial Analysis: Claude Fable 5.2 is now number one on its benchmark for building interactive 3D experiences, at 1271 Elo (452 likes).

Artificial Analysis@ArtificialAnlys
Claude Fable 5.2 is now #1 on AA-3D, our benchmark for how well AI models build interactive 3D experiences

Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) scores 1271 Elo, 67 points ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1204) and Claude Opus 5.5 (1202). Its 95% confidence interval (1246 to 1297) does not overlap any other models, so its lead is outside the margin of error.

Key results:

➤ It scores 132 points above its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1 (1139)

➤ It is ahead of the highest-ranked OpenAI and Google models on AA-3D, GPT-6 Astra (1168) and Gemini 4 Argon (1147)

Google@Google
Today, we're expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two new systems built specifically for the agentic era — bringing our total to four distinct eighth-generation TPU systems launched in a single year.

Linus Ekenstam: Boston Dynamics bolted roller wheels onto its Atlas humanoid so it can drift around warehouses and spin mid-air (89 likes).

Linus ✦ Ekenstam 🔜 Adobe MAX Miami 2026@LinusEkenstam
We have a new contender for the wildest robotics flex of the year

Boston Dynamics just bolted roller wheels onto their humanoid Atlas robot so it can drift around warehouses and hit mid-air 360 spins

their controls engineer literally stopped touching his gaming PC at home because driving the real robot like a video game was way more fun

here's what's actually going on:

> the wheels aren't a commercial product, they're a torture test designed to push Atlas's motors and actuators to their absolute limits

> for the jump 360 spin, the team fed human motion-capture footage into their reinforcement learning pipeline and the robot nailed it on the very first try

> for the side-to-side jump dashes, nobody hard-coded how the skates work. The AI policy figured out on its own how to roll on the wheels mid-slide

> the team drove and tuned the whole thing in simulation first, and it transferred onto the physical robot almost seamlessly

> next up, they're training the RL brain to invent recovery moves on the fly when a motor fails mid-motion

most robotics startups are still trying to get humanoids to walk across a flat room without tipping over

meanwhile Boston Dynamics put theirs on roller skates just to see if they could break the motors
